editorial.rationale: The method itself compresses well — a handful of moves and an ethic — but the book's value includes how the moves feel in use, which needs worked examples. Fifteen minutes carries the method, the examples, the ethic, and the caveats; thirty minutes walks the elements and the modern-discourse argument in full; five minutes is the decision layer. The full book's hundreds of classical quotations cannot be compressed, only sampled.

card.one_sentence: A law dean's plain-language handbook for the Socratic method: how Socrates actually questioned people, how to do it yourself, and why the habit is an antidote to the way we argue now.
card.verdict: The clearest practical introduction to Socratic questioning in print — genuinely useful for anyone who thinks or argues for a living — provided you want a patient handbook of a method and its ethic, not new scholarship or a book of drills.

synopsis.text: Farnsworth explains what the Socratic method is, where it came from, and how to practise it: the question-driven testing of one's own and others' beliefs that Plato dramatised. Working step by step with examples from the dialogues and hundreds of classical quotations, he presents the method both as a concrete technique — eliciting claims, testing them for consistency, welcoming refutation — and as an ethic of patience, inquiry, humility, and doubt, ending with its relationship to Stoicism and its bearing on modern discourse.

core_argument.text: Better thinking is a practice, not a talent, and the Socratic method is its most tested form: question rather than assert, seek the counterexample, treat being refuted as a gift, and hold your beliefs as candidates rather than possessions. Modern discourse rewards the opposite habits, which is exactly why the old method matters more now than ever.

ideas.title: Socrates taught a method, not a doctrine
ideas.claim: The Socratic legacy is a way of examining beliefs, usable on any question, rather than a set of conclusions.
ideas.explanation: Farnsworth's Socrates asserts almost nothing: he elicits what the other person believes and subjects it to tests. The book's premise is that this procedure can be learned like any craft, separated from ancient metaphysics, and aimed at the reader's own opinions.
ideas.representative_example: The dialogues end without settled answers: the method's product is better-examined belief, not doctrine.
ideas.why_it_matters: It makes the book a manual rather than a history: the reader is meant to do this, not admire it.
ideas.caveat: Plato scholarship debates how separable the method is from Plato's philosophy; the handbook smooths that controversy over.

ideas.title: The elenchus: test beliefs for consistency
ideas.claim: The core move is eliciting a claim, then finding other things the person believes that contradict it.
ideas.explanation: Socrates rarely argues that a claim is false; he shows the claimant that they themselves believe things inconsistent with it. The refutation comes from inside the other person's own commitments, which is why it teaches rather than merely defeats.
ideas.representative_example: The recurring dialogue pattern: a confident definition — of courage, justice, piety — is offered, and a series of agreed examples quietly dismantles it.
ideas.why_it_matters: Consistency-testing is the most transferable reasoning tool in the book: it works on your own beliefs, in a courtroom, or in a code review.
ideas.caveat: Consistency is necessary, not sufficient: a perfectly consistent set of beliefs can still be wrong about the world.

ideas.title: Knowing that you don't know
ideas.claim: The method begins from double ignorance: the worst state is not ignorance but ignorance that thinks it knows.
ideas.explanation: Socratic ignorance is a discipline, not modesty theatre: treat your current beliefs as provisional, expect them to be partly wrong, and value the person who shows you where. Farnsworth presents aporia — the puzzled dead-end many dialogues reach — as a success state, because puzzlement is what dissolved false confidence feels like.
ideas.representative_example: Socrates' verdict on his own wisdom: he knows only that he does not know, which is precisely what his confident interlocutors lack.
ideas.why_it_matters: It reframes being refuted as winning, which is the emotional key to actually practising the method.
ideas.caveat: Institutionalised humility can be performed; the test is whether beliefs actually change under refutation.

ideas.title: The method is an ethic
ideas.claim: More than a technique, Socratic questioning is a set of virtues: patience, inquiry, humility, and doubt.
ideas.explanation: Farnsworth argues the moves fail without the character: questioning as gotcha is eristic, not elenchus. The method requires genuinely wanting the truth more than the win, extending charity to the other side, and applying the same severity to one's own beliefs.
ideas.representative_example: The book's distinction between Socratic questioning and courtroom cross-examination: same tools, opposite purposes.
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why the method cannot be reduced to debate tactics, and why practising it changes the practitioner.
ideas.caveat: The ethic is demanding enough that the book's cheerful confidence in adoption can feel optimistic.

ideas.title: The craft of the questions
ideas.claim: Socratic questions have learnable forms: eliciting definitions, proposing test cases, drawing out consequences, offering counterexamples.
ideas.explanation: The handbook chapters teach the elements step by step from the dialogues: how Socrates gets a claim stated cleanly, how he chooses examples that isolate a principle, how agreement is built one small step at a time so the conclusion arrives self-inflicted.
ideas.representative_example: The step-by-step reconstruction of dialogue passages, with Farnsworth showing which move each question is making.
ideas.why_it_matters: This is the practitioner content the title promises: forms you can imitate the next time a claim needs testing.
ideas.caveat: Readers wanting graded exercises will find worked examples instead; it is a handbook in the sense of a guide, not a workbook.

ideas.title: Stoicism is applied Socratism
ideas.claim: The Stoics turned the Socratic examination of belief into a daily practice for living.
ideas.explanation: The book's late chapters connect the method to its most successful descendants: the Stoic habit of interrogating one's own judgements is the elenchus turned inward and made routine. For readers of modern Stoicism, Farnsworth positions Socrates as the missing foundation.
ideas.representative_example: The Socrates and the Stoics chapter, bridging to the author's earlier book The Practicing Stoic.
ideas.why_it_matters: It gives the method a daily, personal use beyond conversation: self-scrutiny as maintenance.
ideas.caveat: The lineage is drawn sympathetically; the real philosophical differences between Socratic scepticism and Stoic doctrine get less attention.

ideas.title: An antidote to how we argue now
ideas.claim: Modern discourse — fast, tribal, certain, and performed for audiences — is the precise inversion of the Socratic habit, and the method is a practical treatment.
ideas.explanation: Farnsworth's cultural argument: social media rewards assertion over inquiry, treats changed minds as defeats, and makes contempt cheap. The method decelerates reasoning, makes disagreement collaborative, and relocates argument from audience to interlocutor.
ideas.representative_example: George Will's summary in the Washington Post: the method decelerates reasoning, making space for deliberation when disagreements arise — an antidote to some social pandemics of our day.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is the book's answer to why now, and the reason readers outside philosophy pick it up.
ideas.caveat: The diagnosis is asserted with examples rather than evidence, and the method's scalability to public discourse is hoped for rather than shown.

book_map.title: What the method is and where it came from
book_map.purpose: Define the subject and set expectations for a practitioner's treatment.
book_map.summary: Socrates as Plato dramatised him, the dialogues as the source material, and the book's promise: to teach the method as a usable craft rather than narrate philosophy's history.

book_map.title: The elements, step by step
book_map.summary: Eliciting claims, choosing test cases, building small agreements, springing counterexamples: the question-craft chapters reconstruct dialogue passages and name the move each question makes, so the reader can imitate the forms.

book_map.title: Consistency, ignorance, and aporia
book_map.purpose: Explain what the method is actually testing and producing.
book_map.summary: The elenchus tests beliefs against the believer's other commitments; Socratic ignorance treats confident not-knowing as the disease; aporia, the puzzled impasse, is reframed as progress — false certainty dissolved.

book_map.title: Socratic ethics
book_map.purpose: Elevate the method from technique to character.
book_map.summary: Patience, inquiry, humility, and doubt as the virtues the moves require; the difference between examining and point-scoring; being refuted as a gift received rather than a defeat suffered.

book_map.title: The Stoics and the present
book_map.purpose: Carry the method forward to its descendants and to now.
book_map.summary: Stoicism as the method turned inward and made daily; then the contemporary case — modern discourse as the inversion of everything Socratic, and the method as a personal treatment available to anyone willing to slow down.

reading_experience.structure: Short, cleanly organised chapters that each teach one element of the method, built around generous block quotations from the dialogues and classical sources with Farnsworth's commentary between them.
reading_experience.voice: Lucid, patient, quietly witty, and unhurried — a teacher's voice rather than a scholar's or an evangelist's.
reading_experience.pace: Even and deliberate; each chapter is self-contained, and the book reads as well in sittings as straight through.
reading_experience.evidence_style: Primary-text scholarship worn lightly: claims about the method are shown in quoted dialogue rather than asserted.
reading_experience.example_style: Reconstructed exchanges from Plato — definitions of virtue offered and dismantled — plus modern parallels from law and everyday argument.
reading_experience.repetition: The core moves recur by design across chapters; readers moving quickly may find the middle reiterative.
reading_experience.prerequisites: None: no philosophy background is assumed, and the Greek terms are explained on arrival.

rating.summary: Strong and near its ceiling for the genre: an exceptionally clear, elegantly written, primary-source-grounded manual for a genuinely valuable thinking method, limited mainly by smoothed-over scholarly debate and a practice component that stops at worked examples.

dimensions.rationale: The method, its moves, and its ethic are explained with unusual clarity; reviewers across the spectrum single out the lucidity, and the step-by-step reconstructions make an ancient practice legible.

For a book whose claims are about what the method is and how it works, the evidence is the right kind: hundreds of primary quotations with the reasoning shown, though interpretive choices among Plato scholars are made silently.
Refutation-as-gift, aporia-as-progress, and the technique/ethic distinction land as genuine reorientations for most readers; philosophically trained readers will know much of it.
The question forms are imitable and the self-scrutiny use is immediate; the handbook stops short of drills or structured practice, so transfer depends on the reader's own discipline.
The method's limits and the difference between examination and point-scoring are treated honestly; the scholarly controversies and the method's failure modes in hostile settings get lighter coverage.
Clean structure and quotable throughout; the deliberate recurrence of core moves across chapters reads as patient to some and repetitive to others.
Documented as unusually elegant for a method book: lucid, witty, patient prose that itself models the clarity it teaches.

meaning.text: The book's deeper subject is intellectual character: it treats good thinking as a set of habits that can be practised, and locates the oldest, best-documented practice regime in Socrates' questions.

lessons.text: Test beliefs — especially your own — against the believer's other commitments; the contradiction is the lesson.
Treat being refuted as receiving a gift: the person who shows you your error has done you a service no flatterer can.
Prefer questions to assertions when stakes are high; questions decelerate reasoning and make deliberation possible.
Hold puzzlement as progress: aporia is what dissolved false certainty feels like from inside.

importance.text: A quietly influential book that became the standard modern entry point to Socratic practice, bridging the Stoicism revival back to its source and giving professions that run on questioning — law, teaching, coaching — their handbook.

author_and_purpose.text: Farnsworth wrote it as the third act of his classical handbooks, after rhetoric and Stoicism: a law dean who taught by questioning for decades, assembling the primary sources into a usable manual because no such book existed for general readers.

strengths: Claims about the method are demonstrated in quoted primary text, not paraphrase.
The reconstruction of question-moves is checkable against the dialogues it cites.
The author's classroom decades with the law-school variant ground the practical advice.
weaknesses: Interpretive disputes among Plato scholars are resolved silently in favour of readability.
The modern-discourse diagnosis is argued by example rather than evidence.
No treatment of when the method fails — hostile interlocutors, power asymmetries, time pressure.

reception.summary: Warmly received across unusually different audiences — philosophers, columnists, lawyers, Stoicism readers — with praise concentrated on clarity and usefulness; criticism is mild and mostly generic to the handbook form.
praise: George Will called it an antidote to some social pandemics of our day.
Rebecca Goldstein praised its elegance and lightly worn erudition.
The Millions called it learned, erudite, and elegant; readers repeatedly cite its exceptional clarity.
criticism: The middle chapters can feel reiterative as the core moves recur.
Some readers wanting a workbook find worked examples instead of exercises.
Scholars note the smoothing of interpretive controversy inherent in the format.

best_for: Anyone whose work runs on questions: lawyers, teachers, coaches, managers, therapists
Readers of modern Stoicism seeking its foundation
People who want a disciplined way to examine their own beliefs
Readers despairing of the quality of public argument
not_for: Readers wanting new Plato scholarship or academic debate
Those seeking a quick-tips debate manual
Readers who want exercises and drills rather than worked examples

is_not: A biography of Socrates or history of Greek philosophy
An academic contribution to Plato scholarship
omissions: The method's failure modes and boundary conditions in adversarial settings
Engagement with contemporary pedagogy research on Socratic teaching
The scholarly controversies over the historical Socrates versus Plato's character
missing_or_weak: Evidence for the modern-discourse diagnosis beyond illustration
Guidance on practising against unwilling or bad-faith interlocutors
A structured progression for building the skill
dated_or_contested: Its readings of the dialogues are mainstream but not uncontested among specialists.

decision.read_if: Read the full book if you want the method properly — the moves shown in the original exchanges, the ethic argued, and a reference you will reread; it is short, beautifully organised, and the quotations are the point.
decision.summary_is_enough_if: The brief is enough if you want the method's core moves, the ethic, and the reasons it matters now, without the worked examples that teach the feel of it.
decision.skip_if: Skip it if you want debate tactics, new scholarship, or structured exercises; this is a patient manual, not a competition guide or a course.
decision.format_advice: Print suits it best: the block quotations and stepwise reconstructions reward a pencil; audio works but flattens the quotation structure the book is built on.

recall_prompts: What does the elenchus test a belief against, and why does that make refutation persuasive?
What is aporia, and why does the book count it as progress?
What separates Socratic questioning from cross-examination or debate?
application_prompts: Take a belief you hold strongly: what else do you believe that sits uneasily beside it?
In your next disagreement, replace your first three assertions with three genuine questions and observe what changes.
Who in your life refutes you well, and do you treat their corrections as gifts or attacks?

workflow.review_notes: Built from the publisher's chapter-level description, the author's interviews, independent professional commentary (Washington Post, Los Angeles Review of Books), a philosophy-index record, and reader reception.

notes: Identity verified against the Godine product page (2021-10-05 hardcover, ISBN 9781567926859, 264 pages; 2025 softcover) and PhilPapers' independent record.

Content fidelity anchored to the publisher's own chapter list (Socratic Ethics, Ignorance, Testing Principles, Socrates and the Stoics) and the author's interview accounts; no chapter-level claims beyond those sources.
Counterevidence and limits recorded: handbook-format smoothing of scholarly debate (LARB), reiterative middle and workbook expectations (reader reception).
Rating scored on content only; endorsements and the author's titles excluded per the rubric.
Narration reviewed against the product contract: no research meta, content-first opening, Greek terms defined at first use in plain language.
Pronunciation: elenchus, aporia, and Socratic names phonemized and inspected before audio; corrections added to the dictionary where the phonemizer failed.
